faq.question: Which files do you need to quote a machined part?
faq.answer: A STEP or native CAD model plus a 2D drawing that marks critical dimensions, finish and any fit requirements. Without GD&T the default tolerance block applies.

faq.question: Can you machine hardened material?
faq.answer: Yes. Hard turning, grinding and wire EDM cover heat-treated tooling steel and superalloys; the route is selected during process planning.

faq.question: Do you support repeat production orders?
faq.answer: Programs, fixtures and inspection routines are versioned per part number, so reorders run from the same documented state.

faq.question: When should I choose bridge tooling instead of production steel?
faq.answer: When the design still carries risk or launch volumes are unproven. Bridge tools carry the part through validation and early sales, then the production tool is cut from the frozen geometry.

faq.question: Can you add metal inserts or threads?
faq.answer: Yes. Molded-in and post-mold inserts, heat staking and machined threads are planned during mold design so access and parting lines are correct from the first shot.

faq.question: What drives the biggest cost difference?
faq.answer: Cavitation, tool complexity and cosmetic class. Wall balance and parting-line placement affect cycle time as much as the mold steel itself.

faq.question: Is printed accuracy comparable to machining?
faq.answer: No. Additive processes carry larger dimensional variance, so critical interfaces are usually machined or printed oversized and finished.

faq.question: Can printed parts be used in production?
faq.answer: Yes for low-rate and duty-cycled parts where material data supports the application. The qualification basis is provided in the material table.

faq.question: Do you support metal printing?
faq.answer: Metal additive is delivered through a coordinated service partner, including depowdering, heat treatment and machining of critical interfaces.

faq.question: What should my drawing define for a folded part?
faq.answer: Material, gauge, inside dimensions or bend centre-lines, bend radius, and which faces are cosmetic. Ambiguity between inside and outside dimensions is the usual source of rework.

faq.question: Can you weld and finish complete assemblies?
faq.answer: Yes. Weldment drawings are planned with fixturing sequence, distortion allowance and finishing masking before the cutting schedule is released.

faq.question: Is there a minimum order quantity?
faq.answer: No. Single prototypes are produced, though batch pricing reflects setup, tooling and programming costs that spread across quantity.

process.title: A traceable path from upload to shipment.
process.intro: Every request follows the same documented stages, whether it is a single prototype or a repeat production batch.

steps.title: Upload and DFM review
steps.description: Geometry, tolerances and material intent are reviewed against live process capability, with a marked-up report returned alongside the price.
steps.note: Typical output: DFM report plus quotation

steps.title: Process planning
steps.description: Setup strategy, tooling, fixtures and inspection points are selected, and any design risk is raised before programming is committed.
steps.note: Decisions recorded against the part number

steps.title: Programming and simulation
steps.description: CAM is generated and virtually verified for collision, stock removal and achievable accuracy.

steps.title: Production
steps.description: Parts are manufactured with in-process probing and machine monitoring, so drift is corrected inside the batch.
steps.note: Work order captures machine and operator

steps.title: Inspection and documentation
steps.description: Coordinate measurement and visual checks are compiled with material certificates into the batch record.

steps.title: Delivery and reorder
steps.description: Parts are packed to specification; the stored process package makes the next batch identical to the last.
steps.note: Repeat orders reuse the approved data

items.summary: A machined aluminium bracket that moved from distorted prototypes to a repeatable single-setup process.

items.background: A structural bracket for an avionics enclosure combined thin walls, large milled pockets and a flatness requirement on the mating face. Early prototypes were within tolerance when loose but moved once installed.
items.clientNeed: Hold a flat mating face and positional tolerance on two precision bores across a 60-piece batch, with material certification and an inspection report for the design authority.

challenges.title: Residual stress movement
challenges.description: Removing mass from a plate blank released stress and changed flatness after roughing.

challenges.title: Bore position after finish
challenges.description: Bores had to stay in position relative to a face that was itself being corrected.

challenges.title: Clamp-induced distortion
challenges.description: Conventional clamping deflected the thin section during the finishing cut.

items.solution: The part was re-planned as a two-stage process with a stress-relief stage between roughing and finishing, and a vacuum fixture that supported the full face instead of clamping at points.
solutionPoints: Roughing left uniform stock, followed by a controlled relief stage before finishing.
Finishing cut in a single setup on a vacuum fixture to hold the datum face.
Bores probed in-machine, then verified on the CMM against the true position callout.
Flatness measured on the relaxed, unclamped part to avoid false passes.

items.name: Diagnostic instrument housing
items.summary: A two-piece polymer enclosure taken from an appearance risk to a stable molded part with a defined process window.
items.imageAlt: Scientist using a microscope in a laboratory
items.background: A benchtop diagnostic device needed a housing with a visible top face, internal bosses for a PCB stack and a seam that read as a single surface from one metre away.
items.clientNeed: Provide cosmetic parts with a consistent seam, controlled boss heights for assembly, and enough dimensional evidence to support an internal validation package.

challenges.title: Sink marks over bosses
challenges.description: Local wall thickness at the bosses threatened the visible outer face.

challenges.title: Seam alignment
challenges.description: Gap and flush depended on both halves and on fastener pull-down.

challenges.title: Late internal changes
challenges.description: The PCB stack was still being revised during tool design.

items.solution: Gate location and packing were set from a filling study, bosses were cored to a rib geometry, and an aluminium bridge tool absorbed the remaining internal changes before production steel was cut.
solutionPoints: Boss and rib geometry revised so cooling stayed away from the cosmetic face.
Bridge tooling allowed design changes without re-cutting production steel.
Shot parameters recorded as the reference recipe for later batches.
Gap and flush measured on assembled units using a common fixture.

outcomes.label: Visible sink on the A-face
outcomes.note: Illustrative outcome of the review stage

items.name: Collaborative robot joint module
items.summary: A compact actuator joint where bearing bore alignment was guaranteed by shared datums and one-setup machining.
items.imageAlt: Parts laid out for assembling a small robot
items.background: A two-axis joint module paired a machined housing with a printed cover and a formed cable guard. Smooth motion depended on two bearing bores staying coaxial once fastened.
items.clientNeed: Deliver housing kits where bore coaxiality survives assembly, with parts from three processes that arrive matched rather than reworked.

challenges.title: Coaxiality across setups
challenges.description: Two bores opposite each other drifted when flipped between operations.

challenges.title: Mixed-process kit
challenges.description: Printed and formed parts needed to fit the machined datum scheme.

challenges.title: Weekly revisions
challenges.description: The cable route changed during development, moving cover geometry.

items.solution: Both bores were finished in one continuous setup indexed from a single datum, while the printed cover and formed guard were toleranced to the housing rather than to the CAD envelope.
solutionPoints: Single continuous setup with in-process probing of both bores.
Fixture designed around the assembled datum, not the loose part.
Printed cover re-orientated for strength along the mounting axis.
Kit-level inspection so all three processes were accepted together.

faq.intro: Practical answers about files, tolerancing, materials and repeat production.

items.question: What do you need to quote a custom part?
items.answer: A 3D model in STEP, IGES, Parasolid or native CAD, plus a 2D drawing showing critical dimensions, finish and any fit requirements. Where GD&T is absent, the default tolerance block for the selected process applies.

items.question: Can you work to a customer tolerance standard?
items.answer: Yes. Inspection plans are written from the drawing callouts, and capability expectations are confirmed during DFM review before a batch is committed.

items.question: Do you supply material certificates?
items.answer: Certificates of conformity can be attached per batch where the grade and supplier support them; the requirement is confirmed at quotation so sourcing matches.

items.question: How do repeat orders stay identical?
items.answer: Programs, tool paths, offsets, fixtures and inspection routines are versioned against the part number and released configuration, so a reorder starts from the approved state.

items.question: Can one project combine several processes?
items.answer: Yes. Hybrid assemblies are planned as a kit, with machining, molding, printing and fabrication scheduled together and inspected against a common interface drawing.

items.question: Is this website a real supplier?
